sections.title: Mission · Control Ownership and Access
paragraphs: Linux security depends heavily on who owns a file or directory and what users are allowed to do with it.
sections.callout: WHO OWNS IT + WHAT MAY THEY DO?

sections.title: Linux File Ownership
paragraphs: A Linux file or directory has an owning user and group. Permission rules then define access for the owner, group members, and everyone else.

sections.title: The Three Permission Classes
sections.callout: U = USER · G = GROUP · O = OTHERS

sections.title: Read Permission
paragraphs: On a file, r allows reading its contents. Directory read behavior concerns listing names, subject to other directory permissions.

sections.title: Write Permission
paragraphs: On a file, w allows modifying its contents. Directory write behavior affects creating, deleting, or renaming entries when combined with needed access.

sections.title: Execute Permission
paragraphs: On a file, x permits execution when the file is otherwise a valid program or script. On a directory, x permits traversal or access through it.

sections.title: Reading Permissions with ls -l
paragraphs: ls -l displays detailed information including file type, symbolic permissions, owner, and group.

sections.title: Breaking Down the Permission String
paragraphs: In a string such as -rwxr-xr--, the first character identifies the file type. The next three apply to the user, then three to the group, then three to others.
sections.callout: FIRST = TYPE · NEXT 3 = USER · NEXT 3 = GROUP · LAST 3 = OTHERS

sections.title: The Dash Means Permission Missing
paragraphs: A dash in a permission position means that permission is not granted to that class.

sections.title: ls -a
paragraphs: ls -a includes hidden entries whose names begin with a dot.

sections.title: chmod
paragraphs: chmod changes file or directory permission modes.

sections.title: Symbolic chmod
paragraphs: Symbolic mode names the class and change. chmod u+x script.sh adds execute permission for the user or owner; chmod g-w file removes group write permission.

sections.title: Three-Digit Permission Modes
paragraphs: The first digit applies to the user, the second to the group, and the third to others. 755 means rwxr-xr-x; 644 means rw-r--r--.

sections.title: chown
paragraphs: chown changes ownership of a file or directory.

sections.title: Directory Permissions
paragraphs: Directory permissions govern listing, changing entries, and traversing the directory. The execute bit on a directory means enter or traverse, not run the directory as a program.

sections.title: Exam Trap · File x vs. Directory x
paragraphs: On a regular file, x means execute. On a directory, x means traverse or access.

sections.title: Ownership + Permissions Work Together
paragraphs: Linux first identifies which permission class applies based on ownership and group membership, then evaluates that class's permission bits.

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: x on a directory → Traverse or access

entries.title: chmod vs. chown
paragraphs: chmod changes permissions; chown changes ownership.

entries.title: Hidden vs. Protected
paragraphs: A dot-prefixed name is hidden by convention, not automatically secure.

entries.title: x Permission
paragraphs: Files execute; directories traverse.

entries.title: Permission Classes
paragraphs: u is user, g is group, and o is others.
